results.title: CJP announces fresh protest in Kochi; From NEET to SIR, is endless street agitation the only political strategy?
results.description: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has announced another protest ahead of Diwali, extending its campaign against the Election Commission of India’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls to Kerala. The organisation has scheduled a demonstration titled ‘Jantar Mantar at Kochi’ at Rajendra Maidan in Kochi on November 7 at 4 pm. The protest will be held under the slogan, “Save Democracy! Cancel SIR!” CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke will participate in the demonstration alongside Vijay Mallangi, the organisation’s South Zone lead, and national secretary Aafreen Nawaz. The latest announcement comes weeks after CJP leaders were detained in Delhi while attempting to organise a demonstration against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the SIR exercise at Jantar Mantar. The organisation is once again demanding the cancellation of the electoral roll revision exercise. However, its transition from a student-led campaign against examination irregularities to a broader political movement targeting the Election Commission raises questions about the direction and priorities of its agitation. From NEET to a nationwide protest movement What began as an online campaign quickly developed into a protest movement following allegations of a NEET-UG 2026 question paper leak. The examination controversy had affected millions of medical aspirants. The NEET-UG examination conducted on May 3 was cancelled following allegations of a paper leak, and a fresh examination was subsequently conducted on June 21. CJP capitalised on the growing frustration and organised demonstrations at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar from June 6. Its central demand was the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, along with compensation for families of students who died by suicide following the examination disruption and withdrawal of cases against protesters. The agitation continued for 36 days. Activist Sonam Wangchuk also joined the movement and began an indefinite hunger strike in support of the students. The campaign eventually culminated in Pradhan’s resignation on July 25. The government also agreed to address the organisation’s other demands, following which CJP announced the withdrawal of its protest. From students to electoral politics The organisation’s latest campaign represents a significant shift in its political positioning. The NEET agitation was rooted in a specific examination controversy, with identifiable demands concerning paper leaks, accountability and compensation. The SIR campaign, however, takes CJP into a much wider political confrontation with a constitutional institution. The Election Commission has maintained that the revision is intended to update electoral rolls by identifying deceased voters, duplicate entries, shifted electors and individuals who are no longer eligible. Such revisions are part of the Commission’s responsibility to maintain accurate electoral rolls. The Supreme Court’s May 27, 2026, judgment in the Association for Democratic Reforms versus Election Commission of India case upheld the constitutional validity of the Bihar SIR exercise. The court recognised the Election Commission’s authority to conduct intensive revisions and held that the exercise had a legitimate purpose. The court also examined safeguards for voters, including notices, hearings, reasoned decisions and an appellate mechanism. It directed the Commission to publish details of excluded voters and allowed Aadhaar as an additional identity document, while clarifying that Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship. The question for CJP is: if the organisation believes that the SIR is being implemented unfairly, why is its central demand the complete cancellation of the exercise rather than the correction of specific errors through the available legal and administrative mechanisms? If eligible voters have been excluded, their cases deserve examination and correction. If there are genuine instances of wrongful deletion, they should be documented and pursued. But demanding the cancellation of an entire electoral exercise without establishing why its underlying process is unconstitutional is a political position, not proof of electoral wrongdoing. The slogan ‘Save Democracy! Cancel SIR!’ may work as a mobilisation tool, but it does not answer the questions surrounding the actual functioning of electoral rolls. Also Read: Bangladesh protests continue as garment workers clash with police; Hundreds of factories shut despite hike assurance Jantar Mantar Episode: From protest to confrontation with authorities CJP’s recent activities have also brought the organisation into confrontation with law enforcement authorities. In October, Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were detained in Delhi after attempting to organise a demonstration against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar at Jantar Mantar without the required permission. The controversy intensified after Jantar Mantar was removed from the list of designated protest sites. While the authorities identified alternative locations for demonstrations, CJP leaders opposed the decision. Das and Ranka subsequently entered the restricted protest area and waved the national flag. Both were arrested and spent approximately a week in custody. They were released after giving a written undertaking before a Special Executive Magistrate that they would not organise another demonstration at Jantar Mantar while it remained excluded from the designated protest-site list. Dipke was also arrested in connection with a proposed Tiranga programme at Central Park in Connaught Place. He was released on conditional bail, with one of the conditions requiring him to ensure that no breach of public peace occurred for a year. These developments raise questions about the organisation’s approach to protest and compliance with administrative restrictions. The right to demonstrate peacefully is fundamental to democratic participation, but it does not mean that organisers can disregard applicable permissions and public-order requirements. CJP now wants to recreate Jantar Mantar-style demonstrations in different cities. Its Kochi programme is the next step in that strategy. The question is whether the organisation intends to build a sustained campaign around documented electoral grievances or keep expanding confrontations with institutions and authorities. Abhijeet Dipke’s AAP connection Another aspect of CJP that deserves examination is the political background of its founder, Abhijeet Dipke. Dipke’s association with the Aam Aadmi Party is not an allegation invented by political opponents. He has himself acknowledged working with the party. In an interview with The Week published in June 2026, Dipke admitted that his previous association with AAP was no secret. He said he had worked with the party several years earlier but claimed that he had no organisational or professional association with it after moving […]

results.title: Bangladesh protests continue as garment workers clash with police; Hundreds of factories shut despite hike assurance
results.description: Bangladesh’s garment industry is witnessing continued unrest as factory workers demanding a substantial increase in monthly wages clashed with police in several industrial areas on Thursday. Police used tear gas shells and stun grenades to disperse demonstrators as protests that had continued for several days in Dhaka spread to neighbouring industrial districts. Violence was reported from Fatullah in Narayanganj district, on the outskirts of Dhaka, where clashes between protesters and police left dozens of people injured, according to media reports. The confrontation marks a fresh escalation in the ongoing labour unrest, with workers demanding that their minimum monthly wage be increased from 12,500 taka to 30,000 taka (approximately USD 245). Hundreds of factories shut amid protests According to Bangladesh’s leading Bengali daily Prothom Alo, police arrested several protesters during the clashes in Fatullah. The unrest has also affected Ashulia, a major industrial zone near Dhaka, where around 100 factories have reportedly remained closed. Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, Superintendent of Ashulia Industrial Police, said authorities were working to bring the situation under control. In another major industrial centre, Gazipur district, workers blocked a key highway as demonstrations intensified, disrupting movement in the area. Meanwhile, Joint Police Commissioner Mahidul Islam said more than 10,000 police personnel had been deployed in Dhaka’s Mirpur area, which has emerged as one of the main centres of the protests, to maintain law and order. The growing police deployment highlights the administration’s efforts to contain the unrest as demonstrations spread across the country’s garment manufacturing belt. Why are garment workers protesting? The central demand of the protesting workers is a substantial revision of the minimum monthly wage. Workers are seeking an increase from the existing 12,500 taka to 30,000 taka, arguing that rising inflation and the increasing cost of essential commodities have significantly reduced their purchasing power. The government has constituted a new wage board to examine the workers’ demands and recommend a revised pay structure. Syed Azad Subhani, chairman of the wage board, said workers would receive their first salary under the revised wage structure in January. However, the assurance has failed to pacify workers, who continue to demand an immediate and substantial increase in their earnings. Workers maintain that the existing minimum wage is insufficient to meet their daily expenses amid rising living costs. Bangladesh’s garment industry employs approximately 4 million people, a majority of whom are women from rural areas. The sector remains one of the country’s largest sources of employment, particularly for women. Garment industry faces major disruption The continuing demonstrations have disrupted operations across Bangladesh’s textile and garment manufacturing sector, with hundreds of factories reportedly remaining closed. Bangladesh has approximately 2,500 garment factories, making the industry a critical pillar of its economy and export earnings. The sector generates around USD 4 billion in annual export revenue, making prolonged industrial unrest a concern for manufacturers, exporters and the wider economy. The shutdowns and transport disruptions could further affect production schedules and supply commitments if the protests continue. Bangladesh’s Unrest: From Sheikh Hasina’s ouster to continuing political turmoil The unrest in Bangladesh cannot be viewed as an isolated wage dispute or a series of spontaneous demonstrations. The country has been grappling with political instability since the student-led uprising that culminated in the ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024. What began as protests over the government job quota system escalated into a nationwide political movement, eventually forcing Hasina to leave office. Her removal was followed by a period of uncertainty, institutional disruption and questions over political stability, law and order, minority security and the future direction of the country. The continuing labour unrest now adds another layer to Bangladesh’s fragile situation. The developments have also raised questions about the role of external actors in Bangladesh’s political transition and the wider geopolitical interests surrounding the country. The strategic importance of Bangladesh and the competing interests of regional and international powers make external influence an important issue for examination. The continuing protests, factory shutdowns, road blockades and confrontations with law enforcement underline the wider consequences of prolonged political instability. Bangladesh’s experience also raises a larger question about what happens when political movements move beyond their stated demands and the country’s institutions struggle to restore normalcy. Prashant Bhushan, Neha Bora’s Bangladesh Solidarity Raises Questions The political messaging around Bangladesh’s uprising also deserves scrutiny, particularly when public figures in India express solidarity with movements there while advocating regime change at home. Prashant Bhushan has made explicit statements supporting regime change in India. During an October 11 discussion on X Spaces, he said, “The only way to get back power is revolution.” He also spoke about the possibility of bloodshed associated with such a revolution. On October 15, he reportedly said, “There will definitely be a regime change. We all want a regime change. Is there anything wrong with that?” Neha Bora, meanwhile, addressed Bangladesh’s Socialist Students’ Front in a video message. Referring to the Gen Z protests, she said, “The Gen Z protests that we are seeing everywhere in this country first started in Bangladesh. And congratulations to you for showing us the way.” These statements deserve serious public examination. What exactly does showing us the way mean in the context of Bangladesh? Is the political upheaval that followed Sheikh Hasina’s removal being held up as a template for political mobilisation in India? And when calls for revolution and regime change are made alongside expressions of solidarity with movements that preceded the collapse of an elected government, what political outcome are their supporters actually seeking? Do Bhushan and Bora believe that the political instability, street confrontations, institutional uncertainty and economic disruption witnessed in Bangladesh represent a model that India should emulate? Do they want India to witness similar upheaval in the name of political change? These are legitimate questions, particularly when the consequences of Bangladesh’s political transition are visible in continuing unrest and disruption to its economy.
